meta.title: Who really said "As a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so life well used brings happy death"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it really is Leonardo — a genuine notebook aphorism (Richter No. 1173). But the familiar English is Edward MacCurdy’s 1938 translation, not the original Italian.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'As a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so life well used brings happy death'?
meta.ogDescription: A genuine Leonardo notebook aphorism — but the familiar English wording is Edward MacCurdy’s in-copyright 1938 translation, not Leonardo’s own Italian.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a real Leonardo aphorism, recorded among the moral maxims of his notebooks (No. 1173 in J. P. Richter’s edition) from the Italian “Sì come una giornata bene spesa dà lieto dormire, così una vita bene usata dà lieto morire.” The exact English wording most people quote is a translator’s — it matches Edward MacCurdy’s 1938 translation, whereas Richter’s older rendering reads “a day well spent procures a happy sleep…” instead.

source.excerpt: Sì come una giornata bene spesa dà lieto dormire, così una vita bene usata dà lieto morire. — “As a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so life well used brings happy death.”
trail: The line is genuinely Leonardo’s: it appears as aphorism No. 1173 in Richter’s edition of the notebooks, whose 1883 wording reads “a day well spent procures a happy sleep… a life well employed procures a happy death.”
The familiar wording — “brings happy sleep… life well used… brings happy death” — is the one listed in Wikiquote’s sourced section as sourced to Edward MacCurdy’s 1938 translation.
The Italian original is well attested: it is reproduced with the same English rendering in reference collections such as the Logos multilingual dictionary.
source.excerptNote: Richter’s public-domain 1883 edition renders the same aphorism (No. 1173) as “As a day well spent procures a happy sleep, so a life well employed procures a happy death.”
source.rightsHolder: Edward MacCurdy translation — Reynal & Hitchcock (New York) / Jonathan Cape (London), 1938
source.rightsNote: Leonardo’s underlying Italian aphorism (c. 1490s) and J. P. Richter’s 1883 English rendering are both in the public domain. But the specific English wording quoted here matches Edward MacCurdy’s 1938 translation, first published by Reynal & Hitchcock / Jonathan Cape, which remains under copyright — so the popular phrasing itself is not public-domain even though the thought is centuries old.

author.name: Leonardo da Vinci
author.heading: About Leonardo da Vinci
author.bio: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was a Florentine painter, engineer and natural philosopher whose thousands of surviving manuscript pages mix anatomy, hydraulics and mechanics with short moral maxims like this one. Because his fame makes him a magnet for invented quotations, it is worth noting that this line is not a fabrication: it appears in his own notebooks. What circulates online is a modern English translation of his Italian, not a verbatim quotation.

misattribution.heading: The nuance
misattribution.intro: Unlike most viral “Leonardo” quotes, this one is real — Leonardo did write it in his notebooks. The catch is the wording: the smooth English everyone shares is a 20th-century translator’s, and it is that exact phrasing (not the older public-domain one) that carries a copyright.

items.why: Leonardo wrote in Italian (“una vita bene usata dà lieto morire”). The polished English “so life well used brings happy death” is a translator’s choice; Richter’s 1883 version instead says “a life well employed procures a happy death.”

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The aphorism sits among the short moral maxims scattered through Leonardo’s working manuscripts, where practical notes on optics and machinery are interrupted by reflections on time, learning and death. Its balanced form — a well-lived day earns easy sleep, a well-lived life earns an easy death — is a classic memento vivere as much as a memento mori.

In Italy the line is a household saying, famously beloved of the science broadcaster Piero Angela and quoted by his son Alberto in tribute after his death — which is part of why the Italian original stays so firmly anchored to Leonardo even as the English travels under looser paraphrases.
context.pull: A well-spent day earns sleep; a well-spent life earns death without fear.
